cards.front: Recall a key point about Local & Regional Government
cards.back: Local government: county councils, district/borough councils, and parish/community councils provide local services. Responsibilities: education (schools), social services, housing, planning permission, waste collection, local roads, libraries, and leisure centres. Funded through council tax, business rates and government grants.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Local & Regional Government
cards.back: Councillors: elected by local residents to represent their ward. They make decisions about local services, set council tax rates, and approve planning applications. Councils are led by a council leader or directly elected mayor (e.g. Mayor of London, Metro Mayors in combined authorities).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Local & Regional Government
cards.back: Devolved administrations: Scottish Parliament (129 MSPs), Welsh Senedd (60 MSs), Northern Ireland Assembly (90 MLAs) have powers over health, education, transport and environment in their nations. England does not have its own devolved parliament - English matters are decided at Westminster.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Local & Regional Government
cards.back: How local decisions affect citizens: school closures, planning permission for new housing, waste collection schedules, library opening hours, parking restrictions, and social care provision are all decided locally. Citizens can influence decisions through: voting in local elections, attending council meetings, submitting planning objections, and contacting their councillor.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Local & Regional Government
cards.back: Challenges for local government: funding cuts (austerity reduced council budgets by 20%+ since 2010), increasing demand (social care for ageing population), and limited powers (councils cannot set income tax or make criminal law). Some councils have effectively declared bankruptcy (Section 114 notices).

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — local & regional government?
cards.back: 1. For Local & Regional Government questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link Local & Regional Government to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate whether local government should be given more powers and funding.

AO1 (Knowledge & Understanding — 30%): You need to demonstrate knowledge and understanding of local & regional government, including key concepts, legal frameworks, and institutional structures. AO2 (Analysis & Evaluation — 40%): You must analyse and evaluate different viewpoints, policies, and approaches related to local & regional government. cards.front: Understanding Local & Regional Government in British Context
cards.back: Local & Regional Government is a core topic in GCSE Citizenship Studies that requires understanding of how the UK political and legal systems work, and how citizens can participate effectively. The specification requires you to know how British democracy functions, understand your rights and responsibilities as a citizen, and be able to take informed and responsible action on citizenship issues.

cards.front: Local & Regional Government and UK Democratic Processes
cards.back: The UK is a parliamentary democracy where citizens exercise power through elected representatives. Understanding local & regional government requires knowledge of how democratic processes work: general elections (first past the post), devolved elections (additional member system for Scotland and Wales), local elections, and referendums. cards.front: Rights, Responsibilities and Local & Regional Government
cards.back: UK citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Key rights include: the right to vote, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to a fair trial, and the right to privacy. These rights are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
